title: Searching in 2D Matrices
summary: Extending binary search into two dimensions needs a different technique depending on the matrix's sort structure — flattening works for a fully-sorted grid, but a row-and-column-sorted one needs the staircase search instead.

slides.markdown: "Search a matrix" problems split into two genuinely different shapes, and confusing them is the single biggest mistake here. A **fully-sorted matrix** (every row continues where the previous one left off, as if flattened into one long sorted array) reduces cleanly to ordinary binary search. A **row-and-column-sorted matrix** (each row sorted left-to-right, each column sorted top-to-bottom, but no relationship between rows) is a fundamentally different structure that needs a different technique — the **staircase search** — because flattening it doesn't produce a sorted sequence at all.

A fully-sorted matrix has the property that reading it row by row, left to right, top to bottom, produces one continuous sorted sequence — the last element of row `i` is less than or equal to the first element of row `i+1`. That means it's really a 1D sorted array wearing a 2D shape, and ordinary binary search applies directly, as long as you can map a flat index back to `(row, col)`.

For an `m x n` matrix, a flat index `k` maps to `row = k // n`, `col = k % n` — integer division and modulo recover the 2D position from the 1D index, with no need to actually build a flattened copy.

slides.sectionTitle: Binary search via row/col index mapping
slides.markdown:
```python
def search_matrix(matrix, target):
    m, n = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
    lo, hi = 0, m * n - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        row, col = mid // n, mid % n
        val = matrix[row][col]
        if val == target:
            return True
        elif val < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid - 1
    return False
```

This is exactly the plain binary search template from [binary-search-fundamentals](binary-search-fundamentals) — the only addition is the `row, col = mid // n, mid % n` translation, done fresh on every comparison rather than by materializing an actual flattened array.

slides.sectionTitle: The row-and-column-sorted matrix: why flattening breaks
slides.markdown:
In a matrix where each row is sorted left-to-right and each column is sorted top-to-bottom, but there's no guarantee about how one row's values relate to another row's, reading it row by row does **not** produce a sorted sequence. Row 2 might contain values both smaller and larger than values in row 1 — the only guarantees are *within* each row and *within* each column, not across the whole matrix.

This means the flat-index binary search from the previous slides is simply invalid here — there's no single monotonic ordering to binary search over at all, and applying it anyway can silently skip over the target.

slides.sectionTitle: Staircase search from the top-right corner

slides.markdown:
![A zigzag path from the top-right cell of a row and column sorted grid, stepping left or down toward the target value 9](assets/staircase-search-path.svg)

The zigzag path is the algorithm made visual: every step is a hard elimination — an entire row or column ruled out for good — which is why the total number of steps is bounded by the sum of the matrix's dimensions, not their product.

slides.sectionTitle: Why staircase search costs O(m + n), not O(log(mn))
slides.markdown:
Each step of the staircase search eliminates exactly one row or one column, never both, and never a fraction of one — so in the worst case, the search takes as many steps as there are rows plus columns combined before running out of matrix. That's **O(m + n)**, genuinely different from (and, for large square matrices, much worse than) the O(log(mn)) a fully-sorted matrix's flat binary search achieves.

This is the direct cost of the weaker sorting guarantee: a row-and-column-sorted matrix doesn't have enough global structure to support a halving strategy, only a one-row-or-column-at-a-time elimination — you're trading a log factor for linear-in-the-dimensions, because that's genuinely all the structure available to exploit.

| | Fully-sorted matrix | Row-and-column-sorted matrix |
|---|---|---|
| Structure assumed | One continuous sorted sequence | Rows sorted, columns sorted, no cross-row relationship |
| Technique | Flatten to 1D index, binary search | Staircase search from top-right (or bottom-left) |
| Complexity | O(log(mn)) | O(m + n) |
| Recognizing which applies | Check: does the last element of each row precede the first of the next? | If that check fails, this is the fallback structure |

The practical skill is recognizing which structure a given matrix actually has *before* picking a technique — reaching for flat-index binary search on a matrix that's only row-and-column-sorted (not fully sorted) is the single most common mistake in this topic.

slides.sectionTitle: Binary search on the answer, applied to a matrix
slides.markdown:
A different pattern entirely: finding the **k-th smallest element** in a row-and-column-sorted matrix. Rather than searching for a specific value's position, binary search over the *range of possible values* (from the matrix's minimum to its maximum), and at each candidate value, count how many matrix elements are `<= candidate` — a count achievable in O(m + n) using a staircase-style walk. If that count is `>= k`, the true k-th smallest is `<= candidate`; otherwise it's larger.

This is a preview of the pattern the last topic in this group covers in depth: binary search doesn't have to search over array indices at all — it can search over any range where a **monotonic feasibility check** exists, which "how many elements are `<=` this value" genuinely is (a larger candidate value can never make the count smaller).

slides.sectionTitle: Using flattened-array search on the wrong matrix shape
slides.markdown:
Applying the flat-index binary search (from the fully-sorted matrix technique) to a matrix that's only row-and-column-sorted is a genuine correctness bug, not just a missed optimization — the flattened sequence isn't actually sorted, so binary search's core invariant (the target is provably within the current window) is violated from the very first comparison, and the search can converge on the wrong answer or miss the target entirely.

The one habit that prevents this: before writing any matrix search code, explicitly verify which of the two structures you actually have — check whether `matrix[i][-1] <= matrix[i+1][0]` holds for every row (fully sorted) or whether that's not guaranteed (row-and-column-sorted, staircase search needed) — rather than assuming from the problem's surface similarity to a simpler one you've seen before.
